1.11.2 ▶

1.1 — Launch: Fork, Clone & Press Play

Today you get the world you will bring to life over the next four months. The sprites are drawn, the tilemaps are laid out, and the player is even animating a walking cycle. But press Play and try to move: nothing happens. The coins do not collect, the spikes do not hurt, and the turret does not fire. You are not handed finished code to read — you are going to read Unity's documentation, break big problems into smaller parts, and build every mechanic yourself.

Setup Lab ~20 min

Step 1 — Fork the starter. Log into GitHub, open the cs-curriculum-main repo your teacher links in Canvas, and click Fork (top right). A fork is a copy of the repo that belongs to you — your commits go to your copy, and you can never break the original.

Fork vs. clone — say it out loud: fork copies the repo on GitHub (server to server, yours forever). Clone downloads a repo to this machine (server to laptop). You do both today: fork first, then clone your fork.

Step 2 — Clone your fork. On your fork's page click the green Code button, copy the HTTPS URL, then in GitHub Desktop: File → Clone Repository → URL tab → paste → Clone. Or if you use the terminal: 

git clone https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/cs-curriculum-main.git

Step 3 — Open it in Unity. Open Unity Hub → Add → pick your cloned cs-curriculum-main folder. The first open takes a while (it imports every sprite and audio asset). When it finishes, look at Assets/_Scenes: you will find Start, Overworld, and Platformer.

Step 4 — Press Play. Open the Overworld scene and press Play. Look closely at your character in the center of the screen.

Tinker: Testing a world without code

  1. What is the player character doing the moment you enter Play mode? Does the sprite stay frozen, or is an animation playing?
  2. Press W, A, S, and D or the arrow keys. Does the player move across the grass?
  3. Look at the coins and the spikes on the map. Walk through the code in your head: if the player cannot move, why can't coins collect or spikes hurt you yet?
  4. Look at the Turret in the overworld. Does it turn, track you, or fire projectiles? What does this tell you about the difference between graphics and gameplay logic?
Tour ~15 min

What is actually in this repo? Find each of these in the Project window — you will touch all of them this semester:

FolderWhat lives thereCurrent State
Assets/_ScenesStart, Overworld, PlatformerBuilt worlds waiting for scripts
Assets/ScriptsPlayerController.cs & package utilitiesBare starter: only starts the walking animation
Assets/PrefabsCoin, Spikes, Turret, Player, EnemyGameObjects with visuals, waiting for logic
Assets/ArtworkTop-down grass, walls, cave tilesFull art assets ready to use
Assets/AnimationsPlayer walk/attack clips and AnimatorPre-wired animation controllers

The course philosophy: You will not be asked to decipher 500 lines of someone else's pre-written code. Instead, we take complex game behaviors (like collecting coins, taking damage, aiming a turret, and jumping) and break them down into tiny, manageable questions:

  • What Unity event triggers when two shapes touch? (Reading OnTriggerEnter2D)
  • How does a hazardous spike differ from a friendly coin? (Comparing triggers vs. collisions)
  • What math calculates distance from a turret to a target? (Reading Vector3.Distance)

Socratic

Why is building a game system from scratch by consulting documentation more valuable for learning computer science than reading a complete, working project and answering multiple-choice questions about what each line does?

Ship It ~10 min

Commit — the habit that starts today. In GitHub Desktop (or git add / git commit -m / git push), commit with the message "1.1a: cloned the starter" and push. From now on: every single class ends with a commit and a push. Your commit history is the proof of your progress.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain the difference between a fork and a clone
  • Open the Overworld scene in Unity and enter Play mode
  • Confirm that the player animates walking in place but has no movement code
  • Locate Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs in the Project window
  • Commit and push your work to your GitHub repository
